static.topic: India–Pakistan Relations and Cross-Border Terrorism
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World
static.whatIsIt: The bilateral relationship is defined by the Kashmir dispute, cross-border terrorism, and a near-absent legal cooperation framework. India's approach combines strategic autonomy, multi-alignment and a firm public stance that talks and terror cannot go together.
static.background: Rooted in Partition (1947) and the wars of 1947-48, 1965, 1971 and the 1999 Kargil conflict. The 2001 Parliament attack and the 2008 Mumbai attacks froze dialogue for years. The 2016 Uri and 2019 Pulwama attacks led to Indian counter-strikes and the Balakot air strike. The Indus Waters Treaty (1960) and the 1972 Simla Agreement remain the principal institutional links.
static.geography: Line of Control in Jammu and Kashmir; the Punjab and Rajasthan border sectors; Pakistan's Punjab province, including Muridke, long associated with LeT's headquarters.
static.socioEconomic: Trade and people-to-people ties have been repeatedly suspended after terror attacks; visa regimes, pilgrim exchanges and cross-border bus/train links have been the first casualties.
static.whyInNews: Proclamation orders issued by an Indian special court against six absconding 26/11 accused, including Hafiz Saeed, remain unexecuted, with the trial of alleged handler Abu Jundal continuing.
static.wayForward: Sustained diplomatic pressure through UNSC sanctions listings and FATF-linked scrutiny, continued pursuit of legal instruments such as proclamation and attachment, and a calibrated policy that keeps humanitarian and trade channels insulated from the terror track.
prelimsPointers: The 26/11 Mumbai attacks (November 2008) were carried out by ten LeT terrorists; Ajmal Kasab was the sole attacker captured alive and was executed in 2012.
Hafiz Saeed founded Lashkar-e-Taiba and later headed Jamaat-ud-Dawa and the Falah-i-Insaniyat Foundation.
The Simla Agreement (1972) commits both sides to resolve differences bilaterally and peacefully.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why legal and diplomatic instruments have failed to deliver accountability in the 26/11 case, and assess what a realistic Indian strategy towards Pakistan should look like.

static.topic: India's Counter-Terror Legal Framework and Proclaimed Offenders
static.syllabusNode: Security — Internal Security
static.whatIsIt: India's counter-terror architecture rests on the NIA Act, UAPA, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) framework and special courts, supported by agencies such as the NIA, IB and state police, with NATGRID and CERT-In for cyber and data-linked threats.
static.background: Post-26/11 reforms created the NIA (2008) and strengthened the legal toolkit. The UAPA was amended in 2019 to allow designation of individuals as terrorists. Trial of the 26/11 case proceeded in a special Mumbai court, producing the conviction and execution of Ajmal Kasab in 2012.
static.socioEconomic: Terror financing networks use hawala, informal charities and front organisations; India has pushed for financial-intelligence scrutiny of such entities.
static.whyInNews: A special court's proclamation orders against six absconding 26/11 accused, including Hafiz Saeed, are still awaiting execution, while the trial against alleged handler Abu Jundal continues.
static.wayForward: Strengthen mutual legal assistance and letters rogatory, pursue asset attachment and proclaimed-offender proceedings systematically, and deepen financial-intelligence cooperation against terror financing fronts.
prelimsPointers: A proclamation order is issued against an absconding accused, requiring appearance within a specified period; non-compliance can lead to attachment of property and declaration as a proclaimed offender.
The NIA (2008) investigates terror offences under the NIA Act; CERT-In is the national nodal agency for cyber-incident response.
Abu Jundal (Sayeed Zabiuddin Ansari), described as a handler of the 26/11 attackers, was deported from Saudi Arabia in 2012 and is being tried in India.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the effectiveness of India's legal instruments against absconding terror accused and suggest reforms to speed up trials and secure international cooperation.

static.topic: UNSC 1267 Sanctions Regime and Multilateral Counter-Terror Governance
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: The UN Security Council's 1267 sanctions committee maintains the consolidated list of individuals and entities linked to Al-Qaeda and the Islamic State, imposing asset freezes, travel bans and arms embargoes. Listing requires consensus among the 15 members.
static.background: The regime dates to 1999 and has been progressively refined, including through the office of the Ombudsperson created to hear delisting requests. India has repeatedly sought listings of Pakistan-based terror figures and entities, and has linked the credibility of the UNSC to its ability to act on such requests.
static.socioEconomic: Sanctions affect the ability of listed entities to raise and move funds, making them a financial as well as a security instrument.
static.whyInNews: The stalled execution of Indian court orders against Hafiz Saeed and other 26/11 accused renews attention on multilateral sanctions and their enforcement.
static.wayForward: Push for stricter implementation of listings by all member states, use the FATF process alongside the UNSC, and continue advocacy for UNSC reform so that bodies reflect contemporary realities.
prelimsPointers: The UNSC has 15 members: five permanent veto-wielding members and ten elected for two-year terms.
The 1267 sanctions regime imposes asset freezes, travel bans and arms embargoes on listed individuals and entities.
India is a founding UN member and among the largest contributors of troops to UN peacekeeping.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether the UN Security Council's counter-terror sanctions architecture is effective in the absence of enforcement cooperation from states hosting listed individuals.

prelims: The 26/11 Mumbai attacks (November 2008) were executed by ten LeT terrorists; Ajmal Kasab was the only attacker captured alive and was executed in 2012.
A proclamation order is issued against an absconding accused; failure to appear can lead to attachment of property and declaration as a proclaimed offender.
Hafiz Saeed founded Lashkar-e-Taiba and later led Jamaat-ud-Dawa and the Falah-i-Insaniyat Foundation; he is a UN-designated terrorist.
Abu Jundal (Sayeed Zabiuddin Ansari), described as a handler of the 26/11 attackers, was deported from Saudi Arabia in 2012 and is being tried in India.
stories.mainsQuestion: Cross-border terrorism remains the central irritant in India–Pakistan relations. In the light of the stalled execution of proclamation orders against the 26/11 accused, examine the efficacy of India's legal, diplomatic and multilateral instruments in delivering accountability.

stories.headline: Bangladesh deploys 108 BGB platoons, tightens border ahead of Hasina's return
stories.summary: Bangladesh has tightened security along its borders and deployed 108 platoons of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) ahead of an expected return of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. Officials cited fears that her supporters could step up violence and sabotage in the coming days. The Awami League, whose activities have been banned, is using online platforms to promote a 'lockdown' programme on November 29 and 30, which Dhaka sees as a possible trigger for wider unrest. The reports are wire-based and developing, with no confirmation of the exact timing or modality of Hasina's return.
stories.whyItMatters: Political instability in Dhaka directly shapes India's eastern border management, trade corridors and Neighbourhood First policy — a recurring UPSC theme linking IR with internal security.

perspectives.take: Frames the build-up as a security precaution driven by fear of sabotage and an online 'lockdown' call by a banned party; the most detailed account of the three.
Same wire report carried under the paper's international desk, headlined around the 108-platoon deployment; adds no independent confirmation of the return timeline.

static.topic: India's Neighbourhood First policy and political instability in Bangladesh
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India & the World; India's neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: India's approach to South Asia built on strategic autonomy, multi-alignment and the Neighbourhood First outlook, under which stable, cooperative ties with Bangladesh anchor connectivity, trade and border management in the eastern subcontinent.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954); post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with major powers. The Neighbourhood First and Act East outlooks gained salience after 2014, with Bangladesh a key partner in connectivity and transit. Bangladesh's politics was upended by the 2024 mass uprising that ended Sheikh Hasina's long tenure; she has since been in India, and an interim administration has been in charge in Dhaka.
static.geography: India shares about 4,096 km with Bangladesh — its longest border with any neighbour — running through West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, with a largely riverine and porous character.
static.socioEconomic: Bangladesh is among India's largest trading partners in South Asia and a major source of migrant labour and connectivity transit; disruption at the border affects trade, transport and livelihoods on both sides.
static.whyInNews: Bangladesh has deployed 108 BGB platoons and tightened border security ahead of Sheikh Hasina's planned return, amid fears of violence and an Awami League 'lockdown' call for November 29–30.
static.wayForward: India should keep channels open with Dhaka's interim administration, separate border-security management from political signalling, and press for the safety of minorities and orderly movement across the border.
prelimsPointers: India–Bangladesh border (~4,096 km) is India's longest border with any country.
India's Neighbourhood First policy is complemented by the Act East policy for Southeast Asian connectivity.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how political instability in a neighbouring state tests India's Neighbourhood First policy and its balance between security concerns and developmental diplomacy.

static.topic: Border security and internal security implications of unrest in a neighbouring state
static.syllabusNode: Security — Internal Security; border management
static.whatIsIt: Internal security covers terrorism, insurgency, cross-border spillover and cyber/economic security, handled through the MHA, intelligence agencies, central armed police forces and state police; border guarding is a core component.
static.background: India's borders are guarded by central armed police forces — the BSF on the Pakistan and Bangladesh borders, the SSB on Nepal and Bhutan borders, the ITBP on the China border and the Assam Rifles in the Northeast. Bangladesh's border is guarded by the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), formerly the Bangladesh Rifles (BDR), renamed after the 2009 mutiny. The India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement of 2015 settled enclave exchanges and boundary disputes.
static.geography: The India–Bangladesh frontier is largely riverine and densely populated, with several stretches lacking physical fencing, making it hard to seal.
static.socioEconomic: Border closures or unrest disrupt informal trade, daily-wage movement and cross-border family ties in West Bengal, Assam and Tripura.
static.whyInNews: Bangladesh's deployment of 108 BGB platoons and its internal lockdown call raise questions about spillover effects on India's eastern border and internal security preparedness.
static.wayForward: Strengthen intelligence-sharing and coordinated border patrolling, complete pending fencing and Integrated Check Post infrastructure, and keep border forces on calibrated alert without disrupting legitimate movement.
prelimsPointers: The BSF guards the India–Bangladesh and India–Pakistan borders; the BGB is Bangladesh's border-guarding force.
The Land Boundary Agreement (2015) between India and Bangladesh settled enclave exchange and boundary disputes.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how political turbulence in a neighbouring country can create internal security challenges for India and evaluate the adequacy of India's border management response.

prelims: Bangladesh has deployed 108 platoons of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) as part of tightened border security.
The Awami League, whose activities are banned, has called an online 'lockdown' for November 29–30.
The BGB is Bangladesh's border-guarding force, renamed from the Bangladesh Rifles (BDR) after the 2009 mutiny.
India's border with Bangladesh (~4,096 km) is its longest border with any neighbour, guarded by the BSF.
stories.mainsQuestion: Political instability in Bangladesh has direct consequences for India's eastern border and its Neighbourhood First policy. Critically examine India's options in balancing security concerns with developmental diplomacy.

stories.headline: PRS State of State Finances 2026-27: fiscal stress across states in focus
stories.summary: PRS Legislative Research has released its report titled 'State of State Finances 2026-27', an annual analytical exercise that consolidates the budgeted finances of India's states into a single comparative picture. Such reports typically examine states' own revenue mobilisation, expenditure patterns, deficit and debt levels, and their reliance on central transfers, allowing cross-state comparison rather than a state-by-state reading of budget documents. The exercise sits at the intersection of fiscal federalism and public finance, since state finances determine the bulk of spending on health, education, policing, infrastructure and welfare. It is relevant as states navigate post-devolution transfer cycles, GST revenue trends and borrowing limits under the fiscal responsibility framework. The report is a research output, not a government document, and its findings are meant to inform debate on state-level fiscal management.
stories.whyItMatters: State finances drive most citizen-facing expenditure, so this report is directly useful for GS-II federalism and devolution questions and GS-III government budgeting, deficits and fiscal consolidation. It also feeds the recurring debate on vertical and horizontal devolution ahead of Finance Commission cycles.

perspectives.take: Frames the story as an evidence-based, comparative stocktake of state budgets — a research institution's neutral consolidation of state fiscal data rather than a government or political claim.

static.topic: Federalism & Centre-State Relations
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union: powers are divided between the Union and States via the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule), with residuary powers with the Union (Art. 248). Fiscal relations — taxation powers, devolution and borrowing — form the financial spine of this arrangement.
static.background: Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) Commissions examined Centre-State balance. The Governor (Art. 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and a flashpoint over assent to Bills (Art. 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Art. 201). Fiscal disputes have similarly centred on the terms of devolution and the conditions attached to central transfers.
static.socioEconomic: States differ widely in fiscal capacity and tax base; poorer states depend more heavily on central transfers, which makes devolution design an equity question as much as a constitutional one.
static.whyInNews: The PRS 'State of State Finances 2026-27' report revives scrutiny of how states raise and spend resources within the federal framework.
static.wayForward: Strengthen cooperative mechanisms such as the Inter-State Council and GST Council, make transfers predictable and rule-bound, and reduce reliance on discretionary, scheme-linked funding.
prelimsPointers: Concurrent List: union law prevails on repugnancy unless state law reserved for President's assent (Art. 254).
Inter-State Council (Art. 263) is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.
static.mainsAngle: Recent spats over Governor's assent and fiscal devolution — assess cooperative federalism in practice.

static.topic: Fiscal Federalism and State Finances
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Government Budgeting, Public Finance & Fiscal Federalism
static.whatIsIt: The constitutional and statutory architecture governing how states tax, spend and borrow: taxation powers under the Seventh Schedule, tax devolution and grants recommended by the Finance Commission (Art. 280), indirect tax coordination through the GST Council (Art. 279A), and borrowing subject to Article 293 and fiscal responsibility legislation.
static.background: The Finance Commission is constituted periodically to recommend the vertical split of the divisible pool and its horizontal distribution among states. The FRBM framework, adopted by the Centre in 2003 and mirrored in state legislation, sets deficit and debt targets. The GST, rolled out in 2017, pooled indirect tax powers and created a compensation mechanism for states.
static.socioEconomic: State budgets carry the bulk of health, education, rural development and policing expenditure; the quality of state spending — capital outlay versus committed liabilities such as salaries, pensions and interest — shapes development outcomes.
static.whyInNews: The PRS 'State of State Finances 2026-27' report presents a consolidated view of state revenues, expenditure, deficits and debt, feeding the debate on fiscal consolidation at the sub-national level.
static.wayForward: Broaden states' own tax and non-tax revenue base, protect capital expenditure from compression, contain off-budget and contingent liabilities, and align state borrowing with transparent, rule-based fiscal targets.
prelimsPointers: Finance Commission is constituted by the President under Article 280, normally every fifth year.
GST Council (Art. 279A) is a constitutional body chaired by the Union Finance Minister with state finance ministers as members.
Under Article 293(3), a state needs the Centre's consent to borrow if any loan from the Centre is outstanding.
static.mainsAngle: State finances are under strain from committed expenditure and limited own revenue — examine how fiscal federalism can be reoriented to reward fiscal discipline without penalising poorer states.

prelims: PRS Legislative Research is an independent research organisation; its 'State of State Finances' report is an analytical compilation of state budget data, not a government publication.
The Finance Commission is constituted under Article 280 to recommend tax devolution and grants-in-aid between the Centre and states.
The GST Council under Article 279A is a constitutional body that decides on GST rates, exemptions and the compensation framework.
State borrowing is governed by Article 293 and state FRBM legislation, which set deficit and debt targets.
stories.mainsQuestion: State finances are central to India's fiscal consolidation story, yet states face limited own-revenue space and rising committed expenditure. Examine how the current framework of fiscal federalism shapes state fiscal behaviour, and suggest reforms to strengthen sub-national public finance.

stories.headline: Tamil Nadu logs ₹1.73 trillion investment commitments; new industrial policy due January 2027
stories.summary: Tamil Nadu has recorded investment commitments totalling about ₹1.73 trillion under the TVK-led government, with industrial parks, renewable energy, automotive and engineering accounting for the bulk of the pipeline. The most recent tranche reported is ₹58,214 crore, led by these four sectors. The state's Industry Secretary, S Vijayakumar, has said a new Industrial Policy is under preparation and is expected to be ready by January 2027. The figures refer to commitments announced by investors, which typically take the form of MoUs and translate into actual capacity only after land, power and clearances are tied up.
stories.whyItMatters: State-level industrial policy and investment facilitation are core to GS-III economy questions on manufacturing, competitive federalism and the investment climate, and to GS-II questions on governance and ease of doing business.

perspectives.take: Sector-focused business daily framing: foregrounds the ₹58,214 crore tranche and the sectoral split — industrial parks, renewables, automotive and engineering — plus the timeline for the new Industrial Policy.
Aggregate, political-economy framing: leads with the ₹1.73 trillion headline figure and attributes it to the TVK government, emphasising scale over sectoral detail.

static.topic: State Industrial Policy and Investment Promotion
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Industrial Policy; Government Policies and Interventions
static.whatIsIt: State industrial policies are the primary instrument through which State governments attract manufacturing and services investment. They offer a package of incentives — capital subsidy, stamp duty and registration fee exemption, electricity tariff concession, land facilitation, and single-window clearance — and are backed by investor summits at which MoUs are signed. Announced 'investment commitments' are therefore intentions recorded in MoUs, not realised capital inflows.
static.background: Indian States have issued formal industrial policies since the 1991 liberalisation, and policy cycles are typically revised every few years to keep incentives competitive. Tamil Nadu's industrial base has historically been anchored in automobiles and auto components, textiles, engineering, electronics and, more recently, renewable energy equipment. The State's current Industrial Policy is under preparation and is expected to be ready by January 2027, according to Industry Secretary S Vijayakumar.
static.geography: Tamil Nadu lies in the southern peninsular tip of India, with industrial clusters concentrated around Chennai, Coimbatore, Hosur, Tiruchirappalli and Madurai, and port access via Chennai, Ennore, Kattupalli and Thoothukudi.
static.socioEconomic: Investment commitments are politically salient because they signal jobs, ancillary MSME activity and future revenue. However, the gap between MoU value and grounded capacity depends on land acquisition, environmental clearance, power availability, skilled labour and market cycles — so headline commitment figures should be read as a pipeline indicator, not as realised investment.
static.whyInNews: Tamil Nadu has reported investment commitments of about ₹1.73 trillion under the TVK government, with the latest tranche of ₹58,214 crore led by industrial parks, renewables, automotive and engineering.
static.wayForward: Track conversion of MoUs into operational units through periodic disclosure of grounded investment, and align the forthcoming Industrial Policy with land-bank readiness, skill supply and grid capacity so that announced commitments are not stranded.
prelimsPointers: Investment commitments announced at investor summits are typically MoUs and are distinct from actual FDI or domestic capital inflows.
Tamil Nadu's manufacturing base is led by automobiles and auto components, followed by textiles, engineering and electronics.
State industrial policies are revised periodically; Tamil Nadu's next Industrial Policy is expected by January 2027.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why State-level investment commitments often exceed actual grounding of projects, and suggest institutional mechanisms to improve MoU-to-capacity conversion.

static.topic: Make in India and the Manufacturing Investment Climate
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Growth and Development; Government Initiatives for Industry
static.whatIsIt: Make in India, launched in 2014, seeks to make India a global manufacturing and design hub by improving the investment climate, easing regulatory approvals and building infrastructure. States compete for manufacturing investment through their own incentive packages and ease-of-doing-business reforms, making State industrial policy a direct instrument of national manufacturing strategy.
static.background: The 1991 reforms dismantled industrial licensing; the National Manufacturing Policy (2011) set a manufacturing growth agenda; Make in India followed in 2014; and Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes were introduced from 2020, initially across 14 sectors, to build scale in targeted manufacturing value chains.
static.socioEconomic: Manufacturing is central to absorbing India's large low- and semi-skilled workforce and to raising the sector's share in gross value added. Investment announcements in capital-intensive sectors such as renewables and automotive may create fewer direct jobs per rupee than labour-intensive sectors, which matters for employment outcomes.
static.whyInNews: The Tamil Nadu investment commitments feed directly into the national manufacturing and investment narrative, with automotive, engineering and renewables among the leading sectors.
static.wayForward: Complement large-ticket capital investment with labour-intensive manufacturing and MSME linkages, and measure success by output, exports and employment rather than by announced commitment values.
prelimsPointers: Make in India was launched on 25 September 2014.
PLI schemes were introduced from 2020, initially covering 14 sectors.
Industrial licensing was largely abolished in India after the 1991 reforms, except for a small list of strategic and hazardous industries.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how State-level industrial policies complement the Union's Make in India and PLI framework, and evaluate whether incentive-led competition among States produces efficient outcomes.

static.topic: Renewable Energy Manufacturing and Investment in India
static.syllabusNode: Infrastructure — Energy; Renewable Energy
static.whatIsIt: India's renewable energy programme covers solar, wind, small hydro, biomass and other non-fossil sources, supported by a national target of 500 GW of non-fossil generating capacity by 2030 announced at COP26 in Glasgow in 2021. States with strong resource endowments, such as Tamil Nadu in wind, attract both generation and equipment-manufacturing investment.
static.background: India's wind programme began in the 1980s and Tamil Nadu emerged as an early leader, with clusters around Coimbatore, Tirunelveli and the Muppandal region. Solar capacity expanded rapidly after the National Solar Mission (2010). Renewables now feature prominently in State industrial policy incentive packages because of their role in powering manufacturing and in meeting clean-energy obligations.
static.geography: Tamil Nadu's wind resource is concentrated in the southern districts and the Aralvaimozhi pass near Muppandal, while solar potential is distributed across the State's drier interior districts.
static.socioEconomic: Renewable manufacturing investment supports industrial diversification and clean-power availability for energy-intensive manufacturing, but grid integration, land availability and transmission evacuation remain binding constraints.
static.whyInNews: Renewables are among the four leading sectors in Tamil Nadu's latest ₹58,214 crore tranche of investment commitments.
static.wayForward: Pair generation targets with transmission evacuation capacity, land facilitation and domestic manufacturing depth so that renewable investment commitments convert into commissioned capacity.
prelimsPointers: India announced a target of 500 GW of non-fossil generating capacity by 2030 at COP26 in Glasgow (2021).
Tamil Nadu is among India's leading States in installed wind power capacity.
The National Solar Mission was launched in 2010.
static.mainsAngle: Assess the role of State-level industrial policy in building domestic renewable energy manufacturing capacity, and identify the infrastructure bottlenecks that limit conversion of commitments into commissioned projects.

prelims: Tamil Nadu has reported investment commitments of about ₹1.73 trillion under the TVK government, with the latest tranche at ₹58,214 crore.
The leading sectors in the latest tranche are industrial parks, renewable energy, automotive and engineering.
A new Tamil Nadu Industrial Policy is under preparation and is expected to be ready by January 2027, per Industry Secretary S Vijayakumar.
Investment commitments announced by States are generally MoUs and are distinct from realised investment or FDI inflows.
stories.mainsQuestion: State governments increasingly headline large investment commitments signed at investor summits. Examine why announced commitments often fail to translate into grounded industrial capacity, and suggest measures to improve conversion while ensuring balanced regional development.

stories.headline: FCC clears SpaceX plan for 1 million satellites for orbital AI data centres
stories.summary: The US Federal Communications Commission has cleared SpaceX to deploy up to one million satellites intended to serve as orbital AI data centres, according to multiple reports. The proposal would place computing infrastructure in space, using solar energy in orbit to meet rising computing demand while reducing dependence on terrestrial data centres and power grids. Some outlets describe the project as 'Starmind' data centres, while others emphasise the scale of the constellation and the FCC authorisation. The decision has drawn attention because a million-satellite system would vastly exceed existing mega-constellations, raising questions about orbital traffic, space debris, spectrum coordination and international space governance.
stories.whyItMatters: UPSC relevance: space commercialisation, mega-constellations, space debris and the adequacy of national licensing versus multilateral space governance under UN COPUOS.

static.topic: Orbital data centres and the governance of mega-constellations
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Space; Space Governance
static.whatIsIt: A proposed large-scale satellite constellation to host AI and data-centre computing in orbit, using solar power and reducing reliance on terrestrial infrastructure; the US FCC has cleared SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million such satellites.
static.background: ISRO (1969) runs India's space programme for communication, remote sensing, navigation (NavIC) and exploration, under the Department of Space. IN-SPACe (2020) and NSIL now promote private participation. Aryabhata (1975) was India's first satellite. Chandrayaan-3 soft-landed near the lunar south pole in 2023. Mangalyaan (2013) reached Mars orbit on its first attempt. Gaganyaan is India's first crewed mission. India is a founder of the Outer Space Treaty framework; UN COPUOS governs space law.
static.geography: Orbital space and ground infrastructure; global coverage.
static.socioEconomic: Commercialisation of space, private participation through IN-SPACe and NSIL, digital infrastructure, energy demand, and equitable access to orbit and spectrum.
static.whyInNews: FCC approval to SpaceX for up to 1 million satellites for orbital AI data centres; implications for space debris, spectrum and governance.
static.wayForward: Strengthen international space-traffic management, debris mitigation, spectrum coordination and transparent licensing; India can use IN-SPACe and NSIL to shape norms and build domestic capabilities.
prelimsPointers: ISRO was set up in 1969 under the Department of Space; IN-SPACe (2020) and NSIL promote private participation.
PSLV is the workhorse launcher; GSLV Mk-III can carry heavier geosynchronous payloads.
India is a founder of the Outer Space Treaty framework; UN COPUOS governs space law.
static.mainsAngle: Commercialisation of space, space debris and India's role in space governance.

static.topic: UN COPUOS and multilateral governance of outer space
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance; Space Law
static.whatIsIt: The UN-centred framework for outer space, including UN COPUOS, which governs space law; relevant to regulating mega-constellations and orbital data centres.
static.background: The UN was founded in 1945 and has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members and ten elected members. India is a founding UN member and a large troop contributor to peacekeeping; it seeks permanent UNSC membership, with the G4 and inconclusive Intergovernmental Negotiations. India is also a founder of the Outer Space Treaty framework, and UN COPUOS governs space law.
static.socioEconomic: Equitable access to orbit and radio spectrum; commercial space investment; developing-country stakes in rule-making.
static.whyInNews: A single national regulator's approval of up to 1 million satellites for orbital AI data centres raises questions about international coordination, orbital debris and whether national licensing can set de facto global rules.
static.wayForward: Strengthen UN COPUOS and multilateral space-traffic and debris rules; ensure transparency, equitable spectrum and orbit access, and coordination among national regulators.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for 2-year terms.
UN HQ is in New York; the ICJ sits in The Hague.
India is a founder of the Outer Space Treaty framework; UN COPUOS governs space law.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether national licensing of mega-constellations undermines multilateral space governance, and assess India's role in shaping rules for orbital infrastructure.

The proposal aims to use solar energy in orbit to meet rising computing demand and reduce reliance on terrestrial infrastructure.
